claim: According to the American Cancer Society, 79,030 new cases of bladder cancer and 18,540 deaths were estimated to occur in the United States alone in 2017.
source: According to the American Cancer Society, 79,030 new cases of bladder cancer and 18,540 deaths were estimated to occur in the United States alone in 2017 (Siegel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Siegel et al., 2017, which is a reference to published work from the American Cancer Society.

claim: Invasive bladder cancer arises from non-invasive papillary or flat precursors.
source: Predominantly of urothelial histology, invasive BC arises from non-invasive papillary or flat precursors, and many BC patients suffer multiple relapses prior to progression, providing ample lead-time for early detection and treatment prior to metastasis (Netto, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Netto, 2013, which provides published evidence for this assertion.

claim: Many bladder cancer patients suffer multiple relapses prior to progression.
source: Predominantly of urothelial histology, invasive BC arises from non-invasive papillary or flat precursors, and many BC patients suffer multiple relapses prior to progression, providing ample lead-time for early detection and treatment prior to metastasis (Netto, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Netto, 2013, which provides published evidence for this clinical observation.

claim: 5-10% of urothelial carcinomas originate in the renal pelvis and/or ureter.
source: Although most urothelial carcinomas arise in the bladder, 5–10% originate in the renal pelvis and/or ureter (Rouprêt et al., 2015; Soria et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rouprêt et al., 2015 and Soria et al., 2017, which provide published evidence for this epidemiological statistic.

claim: The annual incidence of upper tract urothelial carcinomas in Western countries is 1-2 cases per 100,000.
source: The annual incidence of these upper tract urothelial carcinomas (UTUC) in Western countries is 1–2 cases per 100,000 (Rouprêt et al., 2015; Soria et al., 2017), but the disease occurs at a much higher rate in populations exposed to aristolochic acid (AA) (Chen et al., 2012; Grollman, 2013; Lai et al., 2010; Taiwan Cancer Registry, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rouprêt et al., 2015 and Soria et al., 2017, which provide published epidemiological data.

claim: Upper tract urothelial carcinomas occur at a much higher rate in populations exposed to aristolochic acid.
source: The annual incidence of these upper tract urothelial carcinomas (UTUC) in Western countries is 1–2 cases per 100,000 (Rouprêt et al., 2015; Soria et al., 2017), but the disease occurs at a much higher rate in populations exposed to aristolochic acid (AA) (Chen et al., 2012; Grollman, 2013; Lai et al., 2010; Taiwan Cancer Registry, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Chen et al., 2012; Grollman, 2013; Lai et al., 2010; Taiwan Cancer Registry, 2017) that provide published evidence for this epidemiological observation.

claim: Aristolochic acid is a carcinogenic and nephrotoxic nitrophenanthrene carboxylic acid produced by Aristolochia plants.
source: AA is a carcinogenic and nephrotoxic nitrophenanthrene carboxylic acid produced by Aristolochia plants (National Toxicology Program, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the National Toxicology Program, 2011, which provides authoritative published evidence for the chemical nature and toxicity of aristolochic acid.

claim: An etiological link between aristolochic acid exposure and upper tract urothelial carcinomas has been established in several populations.
source: An etiological link between AA exposure and UTUC has been established in several populations (Grollman, 2013; Grollman et al., 2009; Jelaković et al., 2012; National Toxicology Program, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Grollman, 2013; Grollman et al., 2009; Jelaković et al., 2012; National Toxicology Program, 2011) that provide published evidence for this etiological relationship.

claim: Taiwan has the highest incidence of upper tract urothelial carcinomas in the world.
source: The profound public health threat posed by the medicinal use of Aristolochia herbs is illustrated in Taiwan, which has the highest incidence of UTUC in the world (Chen et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2012 and Yang et al., 2002, which provide published epidemiological evidence.

claim: In recent years, more than one-third of the adult population in Taiwan has been prescribed herbal remedies containing aristolochic acid.
source: In recent years, more than one-third of the adult population in Taiwan has been prescribed herbal remedies containing AA (Hsieh et al., 2008), resulting in an unusually high (37%) proportion of UTUC cases relative to urothelial cancers worldwide (Taiwan Cancer Registry, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hsieh et al., 2008, which provides published evidence for this exposure statistic.

claim: 37% of urothelial cancer cases in Taiwan are upper tract urothelial carcinomas.
source: In recent years, more than one-third of the adult population in Taiwan has been prescribed herbal remedies containing AA (Hsieh et al., 2008), resulting in an unusually high (37%) proportion of UTUC cases relative to urothelial cancers worldwide (Taiwan Cancer Registry, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the Taiwan Cancer Registry, 2017, which provides published epidemiological data.

claim: Tumors of the upper and lower urinary tracts have many common features including the somatic alterations that drive their growth.
source: Tumors of the upper and lower urinary tracts differ in important ways, including etiology, but they have many common features (Green et al., 2013), such as the somatic alterations that drive their growth (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Green et al., 2013 and Lee et al., 2018, which provide published evidence for these commonalities.

claim: High rates of activating mutations in the upstream promoter of the TERT gene are found in the majority of urothelial neoplasms of both upper and lower tracts.
source: High rates of activating mutations in the upstream promoter of the TERT gene are found in the majority of urothelial neoplasms of both upper and lower tracts (Huang et al., 2013; Killela et al., 2013; Scott et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Huang et al., 2013; Killela et al., 2013; Scott et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2016) that provide published evidence for this genetic observation.

claim: TERT promoter mutations predominantly affect two hot spots, g.1295228 C > T and g.1295250 C > T.
source: TERT promoter mutations predominantly affect two hot spots, g.1295228 C > T and g.1295250 C > T.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and is based on the study's own findings as well as established scientific knowledge about TERT promoter mutations.

claim: TERT promoter mutations generate CCGGAA/T or GGAA/T motifs that alter the binding site for ETS transcription factors and subsequently stimulate increased TERT promoter activity.
source: These mutations generate CCGGAA/T or GGAA/T motifs that alter the binding site for ETS transcription factors and subsequently stimulate increased TERT promoter activity (Horn et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Horn et al., 2013 and Huang et al., 2013, which provide published evidence for the molecular mechanism of TERT promoter mutations.

claim: TERT promoter mutations occur in up to 80% of invasive urothelial carcinomas of the bladder.
source: TERT promoter mutations occur in up to 80% of invasive urothelial carcinomas of the bladder and in several of their histologic variants (Allory et al., 2014; Cowan et al., 2016; Killela et al., 2013; Kinde et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Allory et al., 2014; Cowan et al., 2016; Killela et al., 2013; Kinde et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2016) that provide published evidence for this frequency.

claim: TERT promoter mutations occur in 60-80% of bladder cancer precursors.
source: Moreover, TERT promoter mutations occur in 60–80% of BC precursors, including papillary urothelial neoplasms of low malignant potential (Rodriguez Pena et al., 2017), non-invasive low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma, non-invasive high-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma and 'flat' carcinoma in situ (CIS), as well as in urinary cells from a subset of these patients (Kinde et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rodriguez Pena et al., 2017 and Kinde et al., 2013, which provide published evidence for this frequency in precursor lesions.

claim: TERT promoter mutations have been established as a common genetic alteration in urothelial neoplasms.
source: TERT promoter mutations have thus been established as a common genetic alteration in urothelial neoplasms (Cheng et al., 2017; Killela et al., 2013; Kinde et al., 2013; Yuan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Cheng et al., 2017; Killela et al., 2013; Kinde et al., 2013; Yuan et al., 2016) that provide published evidence for this conclusion.

claim: Oncogene-activating mutations in FGFR3, RAS and PIK3CA genes occur in a high fraction of non-muscle invasive bladder cancers.
source: Other important oncogene-activating mutations include those in FGFR3, RAS and PIK3CA genes, which occur in a high fraction of non-muscle invasive bladder cancers (Humphrey et al., 2016; Netto, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Humphrey et al., 2016 and Netto, 2011, which provide published evidence for this genetic observation.

claim: In muscle-invasive bladder cancers, mutations in the TP53, CDKN2A, MLL and ERBB2 genes are frequently found.
source: In muscle-invasive bladder cancers, mutations in the TP53, CDKN2A, MLL and ERBB2 genes are also frequently found (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Lin et al., 2010; Mo et al., 2007; Netto, 2011; Sarkis et al., 1995; Sarkis et al., 1994; Sarkis et al., 1993; Wu, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Lin et al., 2010; Mo et al., 2007; Netto, 2011; Sarkis et al., 1995; Sarkis et al., 1994; Sarkis et al., 1993; Wu, 2005) that provide published evidence for these mutations.

claim: Mutations in TP53, CDKN2A, MLL, ERBB2, FGFR3, RAS, and PIK3CA genes are present in upper tract urothelial carcinomas.
source: Mutations in these genes are also present in UTUC (Hoang et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2018; Moss et al., 2017; Sfakianos et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Hoang et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2018; Moss et al., 2017; Sfakianos et al., 2015) that provide published evidence for these mutations in UTUC.

claim: Urine cytology is unable to detect the vast majority of low-grade bladder tumors.
source: Although it has value for the detection of high-grade BC, the test is unable to detect the vast majority of low-grade tumors (Lotan and Roehrborn, 2003; Netto and Tafe, 2016; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Lotan and Roehrborn, 2003; Netto and Tafe, 2016; Zhang et al., 2016) that provide published evidence for this limitation of cytology.

claim: Urine cytology fails to detect the majority of upper tract urothelial carcinomas.
source: Urine cytology also fails to detect the majority of UTUCs (Baard et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baard et al., 2017, which provides published evidence for this limitation of cytology in UTUC.

claim: Currently available FDA-approved assays for bladder cancer diagnosis include the ImmunoCyt test, the nuclear matrix protein 22 (NMP22) immunoassay test, and multitarget FISH (UroVysion).
source: Currently available U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved assays for BC diagnosis include the ImmunoCyt test (Scimedx Corp), the nuclear matrix protein 22 (NMP22) immunoassay test (Matritech), and multitarget FISH (UroVysion) (Fradet and Lockhard, 1997; Kawauchi et al., 2009; Krüger et al., 2003; Moonen et al., 2007; Sarosdy et al., 2006; Skacel et al., 2003; Yafi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Fradet and Lockhard, 1997; Kawauchi et al., 2009; Krüger et al., 2003; Moonen et al., 2007; Sarosdy et al., 2006; Skacel et al., 2003; Yafi et al., 2015) that provide published evidence for these FDA-approved tests.

claim: Sensitivities between 62% and 69% and specificities between 79% and 89% have been reported for some FDA-approved bladder cancer tests.
source: Sensitivities between 62% and 69% and specificities between 79% and 89% have been reported for some of these tests.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and is based on published literature about FDA-approved tests, as indicated by the preceding citations.

claim: None of the FDA-approved bladder cancer assays have been validated for clinical use in detection of upper tract urothelial carcinomas.
source: Furthermore, none of the FDA-approved BC assays have yet been validated for clinical use in detection of UTUC.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and represents a gap in the current state of clinical diagnostics based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: UroSEEK was positive in 83% of patients who developed bladder cancer in the early detection cohort.
source: In 570 patients at risk for bladder cancer (BC), UroSEEK was positive in 83% of those who developed BC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study's early detection cohort.

claim: Combined with cytology, UroSEEK detected 95% of patients who developed bladder cancer in the early detection cohort.
source: Combined with cytology, UroSEEK detected 95% of patients who developed BC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study's early detection cohort when UroSEEK was combined with cytology.

claim: UroSEEK detected 75% of patients with upper tract urothelial cancer.
source: Of 56 patients with upper tract urothelial cancer, 75% tested positive by UroSEEK, including 79% of those with non-invasive tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study's UTUC cohort.

claim: UroSEEK detected 79% of patients with non-invasive upper tract urothelial cancer.
source: Of 56 patients with upper tract urothelial cancer, 75% tested positive by UroSEEK, including 79% of those with non-invasive tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study's UTUC cohort, specifically for non-invasive tumors.

claim: UroSEEK detected genetic abnormalities in 68% of urines obtained from bladder cancer patients under surveillance who demonstrated clinical evidence of recurrence.
source: UroSEEK detected genetic abnormalities in 68% of urines obtained from BC patients under surveillance who demonstrated clinical evidence of recurrence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study's surveillance cohort.

claim: UroSEEK detected 67% of low-grade bladder cancers whereas cytology detected none.
source: The advantages of UroSEEK over cytology were evident in low-grade BCs; UroSEEK detected 67% of cases whereas cytology detected none.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing UroSEEK and cytology performance in low-grade bladder cancers.

claim: A total of 570 patients were included in the early detection cohort.
source: A total of 570 patients were included in the early detection cohort, each with one urine sample analyzed.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's experimental design and patient enrollment data.

claim: 90% of the patients in the early detection cohort had hematuria.
source: 90% of the patients had hematuria, 3% had lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), and 9% had other indications suggesting they were at risk for BC.
evidence: This claim is supported by demographic data from the study's early detection cohort.

claim: The median age of participants in the early detection cohort was 58 years.
source: The median age of the participants was 58 years (range 5 to 89 years; Table 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by demographic data from the study's early detection cohort.

claim: 70% of the patients in the early detection cohort were male.
source: As expected from prior studies of patients at risk for BC, 70% of the patients were male (Siegel et al., 2017; Wein et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by demographic data from the study's early detection cohort and is consistent with published literature (Siegel et al., 2017; Wein et al., 2012).

claim: 31% of patients in the early detection cohort developed bladder cancer after a median follow-up period of 18 months.
source: Patients (n = 175; 31%) developed BC after a median follow-up period of 18 months (range 0 to 40 months).
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical follow-up data from the study's early detection cohort.

claim: The multiplex assay detected mutations in 68% of urinary cell samples from individuals who developed bladder cancer in the early detection cohort.
source: The multiplex assay detected mutations in 68% of the 175 urinary cell samples from the individuals who developed BC during the course of this study (95% CI, 61% to 75%) (Table 1a and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the multiplex mutation assay performed on the early detection cohort.

claim: A total of 246 mutations were detected in eight of the ten target genes in the early detection cohort.
source: A total of 246 mutations were detected in eight of the ten target genes (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the multiplex mutation assay performed on the early detection cohort.

claim: The median mutant allele frequency in urinary cells with detectable mutations in the early detection cohort was 8%.
source: The median mutant allele frequency (MAF) in the urinary cells with detectable mutations was 8% (8.14%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutation analysis of the early detection cohort.

claim: TP53 accounted for 45% of the total mutations detected in the early detection cohort.
source: The most commonly altered genes were TP53 (45% of the total mutations) and FGFR3 (20% of the total mutations; Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutation analysis of the early detection cohort.

claim: FGFR3 accounted for 20% of the total mutations detected in the early detection cohort.
source: The most commonly altered genes were TP53 (45% of the total mutations) and FGFR3 (20% of the total mutations; Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutation analysis of the early detection cohort.

claim: 1.7% of patients who did not develop bladder cancer in the early detection cohort had a detectable mutation in any of the ten genes.
source: At the thresholds used, 1.7% of the 395 patients in the early detection cohort who did not develop BC during the course of the study had a detectable mutation in any of the ten genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the multiplex mutation assay performed on patients without cancer in the early detection cohort.

claim: None of the 188 urinary cell samples from healthy individuals had a mutation in any of the ten genes assayed.
source: At the same thresholds, none of the 188 urinary cell samples from healthy individuals had a mutation in any of the ten genes assayed (100% specificity, 95% CI, 98% to 100%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the multiplex mutation assay performed on healthy control samples.

claim: Mutations in the TERT promoter were detected in 57% of urinary cell samples from patients who developed cancer in the early detection cohort.
source: Mutations in the TERT promoter were detected in 57% of the 175 urinary cell samples from the patients who developed cancer during the study interval (95% CI, 49% to 64%; Table 1a and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the TERT promoter mutation assay performed on the early detection cohort.

claim: The median TERT mutant allele frequency in urinary cells in the early detection cohort was 6%.
source: The median TERT MAF in the urinary cells was 6% (5.76%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the TERT promoter mutation analysis of the early detection cohort.

claim: 98% of TERT mutations in the early detection cohort were at TERT:g.1295228 (79%) and TERT:g.1295250 (19%).
source: Mutations were detected in three positions; 98% of the mutations were at TERT:g.1295228 (79%) and TERT:g.1295250 (19%), which are 66 and 88 bp upstream of the transcription start site, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the TERT promoter mutation analysis of the early detection cohort.

claim: The remaining 2% of TERT mutations in the early detection cohort were found at TERT:g.1295242.
source: The remaining 2% of mutations were found at TERT:g.1295242.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the TERT promoter mutation analysis of the early detection cohort.

claim: TERT:g.1295228 and TERT:g.1295250 mutations recruit the GABPA/B1 transcription factor, resulting in the H3K4me2/3 mark of active chromatin and reversing the epigenetic silencing present in normal cells.
source: The first two of these positions have been previously shown to be critical for the appropriate transcriptional regulation of TERT. In particular, the mutant alleles recruit the GABPA/B1 transcription factor, resulting in the H3K4me2/3 mark of active chromatin and reversing the epigenetic silencing present in normal cells (Stern et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stern et al., 2015, which provides published evidence for this molecular mechanism.

claim: 4% of patients in the early detection cohort who did not develop bladder cancer had a detectable mutation in the TERT promoter.
source: Of the 395 patients in this cohort who did not develop BC during the course of the study, only 4% had a detectable mutation in the TERT promoter.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the TERT promoter mutation assay performed on patients without cancer in the early detection cohort.

claim: Only one of the 188 urinary samples from healthy individuals harbored a TERT promoter mutation.
source: Finally, only one of the 188 urinary samples from healthy individuals harbored a TERT promoter mutation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the TERT promoter mutation assay performed on healthy control samples.

claim: Aneuploidy was detected in 46% of urinary cell samples from patients who developed bladder cancer in the early detection cohort.
source: Aneuploidy was detected in 46% (95% CI, 39% to 54%) of the 175 urinary cell samples from the patients who developed BC during the course of the study (Table 1a and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the aneuploidy assay performed on the early detection cohort.

claim: The most commonly altered chromosome arms in the early detection cohort were 5q, 8q, and 9p.
source: The most commonly altered chromosome arms were 5q, 8q, and 9p.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the aneuploidy analysis of the early detection cohort.

claim: Chromosome arms 5q, 8q, and 9p harbor well-known oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes that undergo copy number alterations in many cancers, including bladder cancer.
source: These three chromosome arms harbor well-known oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes that have been shown to undergo copy number alterations in many cancers, including BC (Vogelstein et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vogelstein et al., 2013, which provides published evidence for the significance of these chromosomal alterations.

claim: Aneuploidy was detected in 1.5% of urinary cell samples from patients who did not develop bladder cancer in the early detection cohort.
source: Aneuploidy was detected in 1.5% of the urinary cell samples from the 395 patients who did not develop BC during the course of the study, but it was not detected in any of the 188 urinary samples from healthy individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the aneuploidy assay performed on patients without cancer in the early detection cohort.

claim: Aneuploidy was not detected in any of the 188 urinary samples from healthy individuals.
source: Aneuploidy was detected in 1.5% of the urinary cell samples from the 395 patients who did not develop BC during the course of the study, but it was not detected in any of the 188 urinary samples from healthy individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the aneuploidy assay performed on healthy control samples.

claim: In 89% of 102 bladder cancers with available tumor tissue, at least one mutation in the eleven genes studied was present.
source: In 91 (89%) of these 102 cancers, at least one mutation in the eleven genes studied was present (in the 10-gene panel or the TERT promoter).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutation analysis of primary tumor samples in the early detection cohort.

claim: At least one of the mutations identified in the urine samples was also identified in 83% of the corresponding primary bladder cancer samples.
source: Moreover, at least one of the mutations identified in the urine samples from these 102 patients was also identified in 83% of the corresponding primary BC samples (Supplementary files 5 and 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing mutations in urine and tumor samples from the early detection cohort.

claim: 62% of primary tumors from patients with false negative urine tests contained a mutation in at least one of the 11 genes.
source: We identified a mutation in at least one of the 11 genes in 62% of the primary tumors from patients with false negative urine tests (Supplementary file 3 and 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the analysis of primary tumors from patients with false negative urine tests.

claim: 62% of false negative tests in the early detection cohort were due to insufficient cancer cells in the urine.
source: We concluded that 62% of the 29 false negative tests were due to insufficient cancer cells in the urine while the remaining 38% were due to the absence of any of the queried mutations in the primary tumor tissue.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that 62% of primary tumors from false negative cases contained mutations.

claim: 38% of false negative tests in the early detection cohort were due to the absence of any of the queried mutations in the primary tumor tissue.
source: We concluded that 62% of the 29 false negative tests were due to insufficient cancer cells in the urine while the remaining 38% were due to the absence of any of the queried mutations in the primary tumor tissue.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that 38% of primary tumors from false negative cases did not contain mutations in the queried genes.

claim: When the three UroSEEK assays were used together, the sensitivity rose to 83% in the early detection cohort.
source: Thus, when the three assays were used together (test termed 'UroSEEK'), and a positive result in any one of the assays was sufficient to score a sample as positive, the sensitivity rose to 83% (95% CI, 76% to 88%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the combined analysis of all three UroSEEK assays in the early detection cohort.

claim: UroSEEK had a specificity of 99.5% in healthy individuals.
source: Only one of the 188 samples from healthy individuals was scored positive by UroSEEK (specificity 99.5%, CI 97% to 100%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the UroSEEK analysis of healthy control samples.

claim: UroSEEK had a specificity of 93% in patients who did not develop bladder cancer in the early detection cohort.
source: Twenty-six (6.5%) of the 395 patients in the BC early detection cohort who did not develop BC during the course of the study scored positive by the UroSEEK test (specificity 93%, CI 91% to 96%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the UroSEEK analysis of patients without cancer in the early detection cohort.

claim: On average, UroSEEK positivity preceded the diagnosis of bladder cancer by 2.3 months in the early detection cohort.
source: On average, UroSEEK positivity preceded the diagnosis of BC by 2.3 months, and in eight cases, by >one year (Figure 5 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the temporal analysis of UroSEEK results relative to cancer diagnosis in the early detection cohort.

claim: In eight cases in the early detection cohort, UroSEEK positivity preceded the diagnosis of bladder cancer by more than one year.
source: On average, UroSEEK positivity preceded the diagnosis of BC by 2.3 months, and in eight cases, by >one year (Figure 5 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the temporal analysis of UroSEEK results relative to cancer diagnosis in the early detection cohort.

claim: Cytology was positive in 43% of patients who developed biopsy-proven cancer in the early detection cohort.
source: Among the 40 patients who developed biopsy-proven cancer in this cohort, cytology was positive in 17 cases (43% sensitivity), and UroSEEK was positive in 100% of these cancer patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the cytology analysis of patients who developed cancer in the early detection cohort.

claim: UroSEEK was positive in 100% of cancer patients whose urines were positive by cytology in the early detection cohort.
source: Among the 40 patients who developed biopsy-proven cancer in this cohort, cytology was positive in 17 cases (43% sensitivity), and UroSEEK was positive in 100% of these cancer patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing UroSEEK and cytology results in the early detection cohort.

claim: UroSEEK was positive in 95% of cancer patients whose urines were negative by cytology in the early detection cohort.
source: UroSEEK was also positive in 95% of 23 cancer patients whose urines were negative by cytology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing UroSEEK and cytology results in the early detection cohort.

claim: UroSEEK plus cytology achieved 95% sensitivity in the early detection cohort.
source: Thus, in combination, UroSEEK plus cytology achieved 95% (95% CI, 83% to 99%) sensitivity, a 12% increase over UroSEEK and a 52% increase over cytology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the combined analysis of UroSEEK and cytology in the early detection cohort.

claim: None of the 299 patients who did not develop cancer in the early detection cohort were positive by cytology.
source: Finally, none of the 299 patients who did not develop cancer over the course of the study were positive by cytology (100% specificity), but 20 (6.6%) were positive by UroSEEK, giving the combination of UroSEEK and cytology a specificity of 93% (95% CI, 90% to 96%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the cytology analysis of patients without cancer in the early detection cohort.

claim: UroSEEK plus cytology had a specificity of 93% in the early detection cohort.
source: Finally, none of the 299 patients who did not develop cancer over the course of the study were positive by cytology (100% specificity), but 20 (6.6%) were positive by UroSEEK, giving the combination of UroSEEK and cytology a specificity of 93% (95% CI, 90% to 96%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the combined analysis of UroSEEK and cytology in patients without cancer in the early detection cohort.

claim: The UTUC cohort consisted of 32 females and 24 males.
source: The gender distribution of this cohort, 32 females and 24 males, is atypical of UTUC patients in Western countries where males predominate (Shariat et al., 2011), but is consistent with earlier epidemiologic studies of Taiwanese individuals with known exposures to AA (summary in Table 2; individual data in Supplementary file 9)(Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by demographic data from the study's UTUC cohort.

claim: The gender distribution of the UTUC cohort is atypical of UTUC patients in Western countries where males predominate.
source: The gender distribution of this cohort, 32 females and 24 males, is atypical of UTUC patients in Western countries where males predominate (Shariat et al., 2011), but is consistent with earlier epidemiologic studies of Taiwanese individuals with known exposures to AA (summary in Table 2; individual data in Supplementary file 9)(Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the study's demographic data with published literature (Shariat et al., 2011) and is consistent with epidemiologic studies of AA-exposed populations (Chen et al., 2012).

claim: Tobacco use was reported by 18% of the UTUC cohort and were all males.
source: Tobacco use was reported by 18% in this cohort and were all males.
evidence: This claim is supported by demographic data from the study's UTUC cohort.

claim: 45% of the UTUC cohort had unimpaired renal function (CKD stage 0-2).
source: Based on estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) values, renal function was unimpaired (chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 0–2) in 45% of the subjects, while mild-to-moderate renal disease (CKD stage 3) or severe disease (CKD stages 4–5) was noted for 43% and 12% of the cohort, respectively (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data from the study's UTUC cohort.

claim: 43% of the UTUC cohort had mild-to-moderate renal disease (CKD stage 3).
source: Based on estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) values, renal function was unimpaired (chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 0–2) in 45% of the subjects, while mild-to-moderate renal disease (CKD stage 3) or severe disease (CKD stages 4–5) was noted for 43% and 12% of the cohort, respectively (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data from the study's UTUC cohort.

claim: 12% of the UTUC cohort had severe renal disease (CKD stages 4-5).
source: Based on estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) values, renal function was unimpaired (chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 0–2) in 45% of the subjects, while mild-to-moderate renal disease (CKD stage 3) or severe disease (CKD stages 4–5) was noted for 43% and 12% of the cohort, respectively (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data from the study's UTUC cohort.

claim: Tumors were confined to a single site along the upper urinary tract in the majority of UTUC cases (38% renal pelvis; 39% ureter).
source: Tumors were confined to a single site along the upper urinary tract in the majority of cases (38% renal pelvis; 39% ureter), while multifocal tumors affecting both renal pelvis and ureter occurred in 23% of the patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data from the study's UTUC cohort.

claim: Multifocal tumors affecting both renal pelvis and ureter occurred in 23% of UTUC patients.
source: Tumors were confined to a single site along the upper urinary tract in the majority of cases (38% renal pelvis; 39% ureter), while multifocal tumors affecting both renal pelvis and ureter occurred in 23% of the patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data from the study's UTUC cohort.

claim: Synchronous bladder cancer was present in 38% of UTUC patients.
source: Synchronous bladder cancer (diagnosed within 3 months prior to nephroureterectomy) was present in 38% of patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data from the study's UTUC cohort.

claim: 89% of UTUC tumors were classified as high grade.
source: Tumors were classified as high grade in 89% of the cases, with the majority categorized as muscle-invasive (T2-T4, 66%; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathological data from the study's UTUC cohort.

claim: 66% of UTUC tumors were categorized as muscle-invasive (T2-T4).
source: Tumors were classified as high grade in 89% of the cases, with the majority categorized as muscle-invasive (T2-T4, 66%; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathological data from the study's UTUC cohort.

claim: The multiplex assay detected at least one mutation in 64% of urinary cell samples from UTUC patients.
source: The multiplex assay detected at least one mutation in 36 of the 56 urinary cell samples from UTUC patients (64%, 95% CI, 51% to 76%; Table 2 and Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the multiplex mutation assay performed on the UTUC cohort.

claim: A total of 57 mutations were detected in nine of the ten target genes in the UTUC cohort.
source: A total of 57 mutations were detected in nine of the ten target genes (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the multiplex mutation assay performed on the UTUC cohort.

claim: The median mutant allele frequency in urinary cells from UTUC patients was 5.6%.
source: The median MAF in the urinary cells was 5.6% and ranged from 0.3% to 80%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutation analysis of the UTUC cohort.

claim: TP53 accounted for 58% of the 57 mutations detected in the UTUC cohort.
source: The most commonly altered genes were TP53 (n = 33, 58% of the 57 mutations) and FGFR3 (n = 9, 16% of the 57 mutations; Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutation analysis of the UTUC cohort.

claim: FGFR3 accounted for 16% of the 57 mutations detected in the UTUC cohort.
source: The most commonly altered genes were TP53 (n = 33, 58% of the 57 mutations) and FGFR3 (n = 9, 16% of the 57 mutations; Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutation analysis of the UTUC cohort.

claim: Mutations in the TERT promoter were detected in 29% of urinary cell samples from UTUC patients.
source: Mutations in the TERT promoter were detected in 16 of the 56 urinary cell samples from UTUC patients (29%, 95% CI, 18% to 42%; Table 2 and Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the TERT promoter mutation assay performed on the UTUC cohort.

claim: The median TERT mutant allele frequency in urinary cells from UTUC patients was 2.22%.
source: The median TERT MAF in the urinary cells was 2.22% and ranged from 0.59% to 46.3%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the TERT promoter mutation analysis of the UTUC cohort.

claim: 94% of TERT mutations in the UTUC cohort were at TERT:g.1295228 (67%) and TERT:g.1295250 (28%).
source: In the UTUC urinary cell samples, most of the TERT mutations (94%) were at one of two positions, TERT:g.1295228 (67%) and TERT:g.1295250 (28%), which are 66 and 88 bp upstream of the transcription start site, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the TERT promoter mutation analysis of the UTUC cohort.

claim: 6% of TERT mutations in the UTUC cohort were at TERT:g.1295242.
source: A third position, TERT:g.1295242, was also involved in the remaining 6% of cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the TERT promoter mutation analysis of the UTUC cohort.

claim: Aneuploidy was detected in 39% of urinary cell samples from UTUC patients.
source: Aneuploidy was detected in 22 of the 56 urinary cell samples from UTUC patients (39%, 95% CI, 28% to 52%, Supplementary file 12 and 13).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the aneuploidy assay performed on the UTUC cohort.

claim: The most commonly altered chromosome arms in the UTUC cohort were 1q, 7q, 8q, 17p, and 18q.
source: The most commonly altered chromosome arms were 1q, 7q, 8q, 17 p, and 18q.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the aneuploidy analysis of the UTUC cohort.

claim: In 90% of 39 UTUC cases with mutations in urinary cells, at least one of the mutations was also identified in the corresponding tumor DNA sample.
source: At least one mutation could be identified in the urinary cells from 39 UTUC cases. In 35 (90%) of these 39 cases, at least one of the mutations identified in the urine sample (Supplementary file 10 and 11) was also identified in the corresponding tumor DNA sample (Supplementary file 14 and 15).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing mutations in urine and tumor samples from the UTUC cohort.

claim: 79% of mutations identified in urinary cells from UTUC patients were also identified in the corresponding tumor sample.
source: When all 80 mutations identified in the urinary cells were considered, 63 (79%) were identified in the corresponding tumor sample.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing mutations in urine and tumor samples from the UTUC cohort.

claim: 96% of chromosomal gains or losses observed in urinary cells from UTUC patients were also observed in the primary tumors.
source: Overall, 96% of the chromosomal gains or losses observed in the urinary cells were also observed in the primary tumors (Supplementary file 13).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing aneuploidy in urine and tumor samples from the UTUC cohort.

claim: Only 4 of 17 urine samples from UTUC patients without detectable mutations were from patients whose tumors did not contain any of the queried mutations.
source: From the evaluation of the primary tumor samples, we found that only four (24%) of these 17 urine samples were from patients whose tumors did not contain any of the queried mutations (Supplementary file 14 and 15).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the analysis of primary tumors from UTUC patients with false negative urine tests.

claim: 76% of failures of the mutation test in UTUC were due to insufficient number of cancer cells in the urine.
source: Thus, we concluded that the main reason for failure of the mutation test was an insufficient number of cancer cells in the urine, which accounted for 13 (76%) of the 17 failures.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that 76% of primary tumors from false negative cases contained mutations.

claim: When the three UroSEEK assays were used together, the sensitivity rose to 75% in the UTUC cohort.
source: Thus, when the three assays were used together, and a positive result in any one assay was sufficient to score a sample as positive, the sensitivity rose to 75% (95% CI 62.2% to 84.6%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the combined analysis of all three UroSEEK assays in the UTUC cohort.

claim: UroSEEK was positive in 79% of patients with stage Ta/T1 UTUC tumors.
source: The test was positive in 15 (79%) of 19 patients with stage Ta/T1 tumors and 27 (73%) of 37 patients with stage T2-T4 tumors (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the UroSEEK analysis stratified by tumor stage in the UTUC cohort.

claim: UroSEEK was positive in 73% of patients with stage T2-T4 UTUC tumors.
source: The test was positive in 15 (79%) of 19 patients with stage Ta/T1 tumors and 27 (73%) of 37 patients with stage T2-T4 tumors (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the UroSEEK analysis stratified by tumor stage in the UTUC cohort.

claim: Cytology was positive in 9.5% of UTUC cases where cytology was available.
source: Cytology was available in 42 cases, and of these, four (9.5%) were positive on cytology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the cytology analysis of the UTUC cohort.

claim: UroSEEK detected all four UTUC cases that were positive on cytology.
source: Cytology was available in 42 cases, and of these, four (9.5%) were positive on cytology. UroSEEK detected all four of these cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing UroSEEK and cytology results in the UTUC cohort.

claim: UroSEEK was positive in 5 of 7 UTUC cases that had an equivocal cytology diagnosis of suspicious for malignancy.
source: In addition, UroSEEK was positive in 5/7 cases that had an equivocal cytology diagnosis of suspicious for malignancy, and 22/31 samples that were negative on cytology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing UroSEEK and cytology results in the UTUC cohort.

claim: UroSEEK was positive in 22 of 31 UTUC samples that were negative on cytology.
source: In addition, UroSEEK was positive in 5/7 cases that had an equivocal cytology diagnosis of suspicious for malignancy, and 22/31 samples that were negative on cytology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing UroSEEK and cytology results in the UTUC cohort.

claim: All but two of the 56 UTUC patients had detectable aristolactam-DNA adducts.
source: All but two of the 56 patients had detectable aristolactam (AL)-DNA adducts (Table 2) with levels ranging from 0.4 to 68 dA-AL-I adducts per 108 nucleotides.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis of renal cortical DNA adducts in the UTUC cohort.

claim: Aristolactam-DNA adduct levels in UTUC patients ranged from 0.4 to 68 dA-AL-I adducts per 10^8 nucleotides.
source: All but two of the 56 patients had detectable aristolactam (AL)-DNA adducts (Table 2) with levels ranging from 0.4 to 68 dA-AL-I adducts per 108 nucleotides.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis of renal cortical DNA adducts in the UTUC cohort.

claim: The A > T signature mutation associated with aristolochic acid was highly represented in the mutational spectra of TP53 (18/32 A > T) and HRAS (2/2 A > T) found in urinary cells from UTUC patients.
source: Moreover, the A > T signature mutation (Hoang et al., 2013) associated with AA was highly represented in the mutational spectra of TP53 (18/32 A > T) and HRAS (2/2 A > T) found in urinary cells (Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutation analysis of urinary cells in the UTUC cohort and is consistent with the known mutational signature of aristolochic acid (Hoang et al., 2013).

claim: The activated metabolites of aristolochic acid bind covalently to the exocyclic amino groups in purine bases, with a preference for dA, leading to characteristic A > T transversions.
source: The activated metabolites of AA bind covalently to the exocyclic amino groups in purine bases, with a preference for dA, leading to characteristic A > T transversions (Hollstein et al., 2013; Moriya et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hollstein et al., 2013 and Moriya et al., 2011, which provide published evidence for the molecular mechanism of aristolochic acid mutagenesis.

claim: 322 patients with a bladder cancer tumor containing a mutation in at least one of the 11 genes were evaluated in the surveillance cohort.
source: We evaluated a total of 322 patients with a BC tumor containing a mutation in at least one of the 11 genes and a urine sample collected within 0–5 years after surgery.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's experimental design and patient enrollment data for the surveillance cohort.

claim: 58% of patients in the surveillance cohort developed clinically evident bladder cancer after a median follow-up period of 10.7 months.
source: In 187 (58%) of the 322 patients, clinically evident BC developed after a median follow-up period of 10.7 months (range 0 to 51 months).
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical follow-up data from the study's surveillance cohort.

claim: The median age of participants in the surveillance cohort was 62 years.
source: The median age of the participants was 62 years (range 20 to 93), and 75% of the patients were male as expected from the demographics of BC.
evidence: This claim is supported by demographic data from the study's surveillance cohort.

claim: 75% of patients in the surveillance cohort were male.
source: The median age of the participants was 62 years (range 20 to 93), and 75% of the patients were male as expected from the demographics of BC.
evidence: This claim is supported by demographic data from the study's surveillance cohort.

claim: The multiplex assay detected mutations in 52% of urinary cell samples from patients who developed recurrent bladder cancer in the surveillance cohort.
source: The multiplex assay detected mutations in 52% of the urinary cell samples from patients who developed recurrent BC during the study interval (95% CI, 45% to 60%; Supplementary file 16 and Supplementary file 17).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the multiplex mutation assay performed on the surveillance cohort.

claim: The median mutant allele frequency in urinary cells with detectable mutations in the surveillance cohort was 7%.
source: The median MAF in the urinary cells with detectable mutations was 7% (6.89%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutation analysis of the surveillance cohort.

claim: FGFR3 accounted for 43% of the 134 mutations detected in the surveillance cohort.
source: The most commonly altered genes were FGFR3 (43% of the 134 mutations) and TP53 (30% of the 134 mutations; Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutation analysis of the surveillance cohort.

claim: TP53 accounted for 30% of the 134 mutations detected in the surveillance cohort.
source: The most commonly altered genes were FGFR3 (43% of the 134 mutations) and TP53 (30% of the 134 mutations; Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutation analysis of the surveillance cohort.

claim: 7% of patients who did not develop recurrent bladder cancer in the surveillance cohort had a detectable mutation in their urinary cell sample.
source: Some cases were however considered to be false positives; 7% of the 135 patients who did not develop recurrent BC during the course of the study had a detectable mutation in their urinary cell sample (see Discussion).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the multiplex mutation assay performed on patients without recurrence in the surveillance cohort.

claim: The mean interval between a positive multiplex assay test and the diagnosis of recurrent bladder cancer in the surveillance cohort was 7 months.
source: The mean interval between a positive multiplex assay test and the diagnosis of recurrent BC was 7 months (range 0 to 51 months).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the temporal analysis of multiplex assay results relative to cancer recurrence in the surveillance cohort.

claim: Mutations in the TERT promoter were detected in 57% of urinary cell samples from patients who developed recurrent bladder cancer in the surveillance cohort.
source: Mutations in the TERT promoter were detected in 57% of the urinary cell samples from patients who developed recurrent BC during the study interval (95% CI 44% to 58%; (Table 1b and Supplementary file 18).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the TERT promoter mutation assay performed on the surveillance cohort.

claim: The median TERT mutant allele frequency in urinary cells with detectable mutations in the surveillance cohort was 5%.
source: The median TERT MAF in the urinary cells with detectable mutations was 5% (5.02%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the TERT promoter mutation analysis of the surveillance cohort.

claim: The mean interval between a positive TERT test and the diagnosis of recurrent bladder cancer in the surveillance cohort was 7 months.
source: The mean interval between a positive TERT test and the diagnosis of recurrent BC was 7 months (range 0 to 40 months).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the temporal analysis of TERT promoter assay results relative to cancer recurrence in the surveillance cohort.

claim: 10% of patients who did not develop recurrent bladder cancer in the surveillance cohort had a detectable TERT promoter mutation in their urine sample.
source: Some results were considered to be false positives; 10% (95% CI, 83% to 94%) of the 135 patients who did not develop recurrent BC during the course of the study had a detectable TERT promoter mutation in their urine sample.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the TERT promoter mutation assay performed on patients without recurrence in the surveillance cohort.

claim: Aneuploidy was detected in 28% of urinary cell samples from patients who developed recurrent bladder cancer in the surveillance cohort.
source: Aneuploidy was detected in 28% (95% CI 24% to 37%) of the urinary cell samples from the patients who developed recurrent BC during the course of the study (Table 1b and Supplementary file 19).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the aneuploidy assay performed on the surveillance cohort.

claim: The most commonly altered chromosome arms in the surveillance cohort were 8p, 8q, and 9p.
source: The most commonly altered chromosome arms were 8 p, 8q, and 9 p, as in the early detection cohort.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the aneuploidy analysis of the surveillance cohort.

claim: 2% of patients who did not develop recurrent bladder cancer in the surveillance cohort exhibited aneuploidy in at least one of their urinary cell samples.
source: In this assay, only 2% of the 135 patients who did not develop recurrent BC during the course of the study exhibited aneuploidy in at least one of their urinary cell samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the aneuploidy assay performed on patients without recurrence in the surveillance cohort.

claim: The sensitivity of UroSEEK was 68% in the surveillance cohort.
source: Thus, the sensitivity of UroSEEK was 68% (95% CI, 59% to 73%; Table 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the combined analysis of all three UroSEEK assays in the surveillance cohort.

claim: UroSEEK had a specificity of 80% in the surveillance cohort.
source: Twenty percent of the 135 patients in this cohort who did not develop BC during the course of the study scored positive by the UroSEEK test, yielding a specificity of 80% (95% CI, 77% to 91%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the UroSEEK analysis of patients without recurrence in the surveillance cohort.

claim: On average, UroSEEK positivity preceded the diagnosis of bladder cancer by 7 months in the surveillance cohort.
source: On average, UroSEEK positivity preceded the diagnosis of BC by 7 months, and in 47 cases, by >one year (Figure 4 and Supplementary file 16).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the temporal analysis of UroSEEK results relative to cancer recurrence in the surveillance cohort.

claim: In 47 cases in the surveillance cohort, UroSEEK positivity preceded the diagnosis of bladder cancer by more than one year.
source: On average, UroSEEK positivity preceded the diagnosis of BC by 7 months, and in 47 cases, by >one year (Figure 4 and Supplementary file 16).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the temporal analysis of UroSEEK results relative to cancer recurrence in the surveillance cohort.

claim: 25% of patients who developed recurrent bladder cancer in the surveillance cohort were positive by cytology.
source: Among the 120 patients who developed recurrent BC in this cohort, 30 (25%) were positive by cytology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the cytology analysis of patients with recurrent cancer in the surveillance cohort.

claim: No positive cytology results were observed in surveillance cohort patients without recurrent tumors.
source: Conversely, no positive cytology results were observed in patients without recurrent tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the cytology analysis of patients without recurrence in the surveillance cohort.

claim: UroSEEK was positive in 90% of recurrent bladder cancer patients with urines positive by cytology in the surveillance cohort.
source: UroSEEK was positive in 90% of the recurrent BC patients with urines positive by cytology and in 61% of the 90 recurrent BC patients with urines negative by cytology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing UroSEEK and cytology results in the surveillance cohort.

claim: UroSEEK was positive in 61% of recurrent bladder cancer patients with urines negative by cytology in the surveillance cohort.
source: UroSEEK was positive in 90% of the recurrent BC patients with urines positive by cytology and in 61% of the 90 recurrent BC patients with urines negative by cytology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing UroSEEK and cytology results in the surveillance cohort.

claim: UroSEEK plus cytology achieved 71% sensitivity in the surveillance cohort.
source: Thus, in combination, UroSEEK plus cytology achieved 71% sensitivity (95% CI, 61.84% to 78.77; Figure 2 and Supplementary files 17, 18, 19).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the combined analysis of UroSEEK and cytology in the surveillance cohort.

claim: UroSEEK plus cytology had a specificity of 82% in the surveillance cohort.
source: Among the 76 patients with cytology who did not develop recurrent BC during the course of the study, 18% scored as positive by either cytology or UroSEEK, which yielded a specificity of 82% (95% CI, 71% to 90%; see Discussion).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the combined analysis of UroSEEK and cytology in patients without recurrence in the surveillance cohort.

claim: Cytology detected none of 49 low-grade bladder tumors evaluated in the study.
source: Cytology was available for 49 low-grade tumors evaluated in this study (six from the early detection cohort and 43 from the Surveillance cohort). None of these low-grade tumors, however, were detected by cytology (0% sensitivity; 95% CI, 0.0% to 6.7%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the cytology analysis of low-grade tumors across both cohorts.

claim: UroSEEK detected 67% of low-grade bladder tumors.
source: In contrast, UroSEEK detected 67% (95% CI 51% to 81%) of the low-grade tumors (identical rate of 67% in both cohorts; Supplementary file 20 and Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the UroSEEK analysis of low-grade tumors across both cohorts.

claim: Cytology was positive in 45% of 102 high-grade bladder tumors evaluated in the study.
source: Cytology was also available for 102 high-grade tumors (in situ urothelial carcinoma, non-invasive high-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma or infiltrating high-grade urothelial carcinoma) evaluated in this study (early detection cohort, n = 34, and BC Surveillance cohort, n = 68). Cytology was positive in 45% of these patients (50% and 41% in the early detection and BC surveillance cohorts, respectively) while UroSEEK was positive in 80% (100% and 71% in the early detection and surveillance cohorts, respectively; Supplementary file 2 and 16).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the cytology analysis of high-grade tumors across both cohorts.

claim: UroSEEK was positive in 80% of high-grade bladder tumors.
source: Cytology was also available for 102 high-grade tumors (in situ urothelial carcinoma, non-invasive high-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma or infiltrating high-grade urothelial carcinoma) evaluated in this study (early detection cohort, n = 34, and BC Surveillance cohort, n = 68). Cytology was positive in 45% of these patients (50% and 41% in the early detection and BC surveillance cohorts, respectively) while UroSEEK was positive in 80% (100% and 71% in the early detection and surveillance cohorts, respectively; Supplementary file 2 and 16).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the UroSEEK analysis of high-grade tumors across both cohorts.

claim: All 51 patients in the early detection cohort whose urine samples were positive by cytology developed biopsy-proven bladder cancer.
source: This specificity was verified in our study: all 51 patients in the BC early detection cohort whose urine samples were positive by cytology developed biopsy-proven BC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the cytology analysis and clinical follow-up in the early detection cohort.

claim: UroSEEK raised the sensitivity of cytology from 43% to 95% in the early detection cohort.
source: UroSEEK adds considerably to sensitivity, as it raised the sensitivity of cytology from 43% to 95% in the BC early detection cohort, from 25% to 71% in the BC Surveillance cohort, and from 10% to 75% in the UTUC cohort.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the performance of cytology alone versus UroSEEK plus cytology in the early detection cohort.

claim: UroSEEK raised the sensitivity of cytology from 25% to 71% in the surveillance cohort.
source: UroSEEK adds considerably to sensitivity, as it raised the sensitivity of cytology from 43% to 95% in the BC early detection cohort, from 25% to 71% in the BC Surveillance cohort, and from 10% to 75% in the UTUC cohort.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the performance of cytology alone versus UroSEEK plus cytology in the surveillance cohort.

claim: UroSEEK raised the sensitivity of cytology from 10% to 75% in the UTUC cohort.
source: UroSEEK adds considerably to sensitivity, as it raised the sensitivity of cytology from 43% to 95% in the BC early detection cohort, from 25% to 71% in the BC Surveillance cohort, and from 10% to 75% in the UTUC cohort.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the performance of cytology alone versus UroSEEK plus cytology in the UTUC cohort.

claim: UroSEEK correctly identified 80% of low-grade upper tract urothelial carcinomas while none were detected by cytology.
source: Similarly, UroSEEK correctly identified 80% of low-grade UTUC while none were detected by cytology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing UroSEEK and cytology performance in low-grade UTUC.

claim: In the early detection cohort, 105 urine samples were scored as 'atypical' by cytology.
source: In the BC early detection cohort, for example, 105 urine samples were scored as 'atypical', and of these cases, 19% developed recurrence while the other 81% did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the cytology analysis of the early detection cohort.

claim: 19% of atypical cytology cases in the early detection cohort developed recurrence.
source: In the BC early detection cohort, for example, 105 urine samples were scored as 'atypical', and of these cases, 19% developed recurrence while the other 81% did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the cytology analysis and clinical follow-up in the early detection cohort.

claim: UroSEEK was positive in 95% of atypical cytology cases that developed bladder cancer.
source: UroSEEK was positive in 95% of the atypical cases that developed BC, but only in 13% of the atypical cases that did not develop cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the UroSEEK analysis of atypical cytology cases in the early detection cohort.

claim: UroSEEK was positive in only 13% of atypical cytology cases that did not develop bladder cancer.
source: UroSEEK was positive in 95% of the atypical cases that developed BC, but only in 13% of the atypical cases that did not develop cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the UroSEEK analysis of atypical cytology cases in the early detection cohort.

claim: Mutations were detected in 93% of urinary cell DNA samples compared to 36% of plasma samples from 14 UTUC patients.
source: Mutations were detected in 93% (13/14) of the urinary cell DNA samples compared to 36% (5/14) of the plasma samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing mutation detection in matched urine and plasma samples from UTUC patients.

claim: The plasma test failed to identify any of the six non-muscle-invasive UTUC cancers while all six were identified in the matched urinary cell DNA samples.
source: Importantly, the plasma test failed to identify any of the six non-muscle-invasive cancers (Ta/T1), while all six (100%) were identified in the matched urinary cell DNA samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing mutation detection in matched urine and plasma samples from UTUC patients with non-muscle-invasive cancers.

claim: The median mutant allele frequency in plasma when a mutation was detectable was only 0.3% compared to 15% in urinary cells.
source: The superior performance in urinary cells was likely due to a substantial enrichment for mutated DNA in these cells compared to plasma; the median MAF in plasma when a mutation was detectable was only 0.3% compared to 15% in the urinary cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing mutant allele frequencies in matched urine and plasma samples from UTUC patients.

claim: In large population-based studies involving over 80,000 individuals participating in health screening, the fraction of individuals with micro-hematuria ranged from 2.4% to 31.1%.
source: In large population-based studies involving over 80,000 individuals participating in health screening, the fraction of individuals with micro-hematuria ranged from 2.4% to 31.1% (Davis et al., 2012; Wein et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Davis et al., 2012 and Wein et al., 2012, which provide published epidemiological data.

claim: It has been estimated that 5% of patients with microscopic hematuria actually have urothelial cancer.
source: It has been estimated that 5% of such patients actually have urothelial cancer (Khadra et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Khadra et al., 2000, which provides published epidemiological data.

claim: UroSEEK plus cytology extrapolates to a positive predictive value of 66% and a negative predictive value of 99.3% for bladder cancer in patients with microscopic hematuria or dysuria.
source: In the current study, UroSEEK plus cytology had a sensitivity of 95% and a specificity of 93% for BC in patients with this presentation. These results extrapolate to a positive predictive value (PPV) of 66% (95% CI, 55% to 74%) and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 99.3% (95% CI, 97.3% to 99.8%).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical calculations using the sensitivity and specificity data from the study combined with published prevalence estimates.

claim: A mutation in at least one of the 11 queried genes was present in 95.2% of bladder cancers evaluated.
source: For example, we found during the course of this study that a mutation in at least one of the 11 queried genes was present in 95.2% of BCs evaluated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutation analysis of bladder cancer tumors in the study.

claim: Ten-year cancer specific survival rates show that 91% of patients with stage T1 upper tract urothelial carcinomas are expected to be cured by surgery.
source: In UTUC, ten-year cancer specific survival rates show that 91% of patients with stage T1 malignancies are expected to be cured by surgery, compared to only 78%, 34% and 0% of patients with stage T2, T3, or T4 tumors, respectively (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2008, which provides published survival data.

claim: 78% of patients with stage T2 upper tract urothelial carcinomas are expected to be cured by surgery.
source: In UTUC, ten-year cancer specific survival rates show that 91% of patients with stage T1 malignancies are expected to be cured by surgery, compared to only 78%, 34% and 0% of patients with stage T2, T3, or T4 tumors, respectively (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2008, which provides published survival data.

claim: 34% of patients with stage T3 upper tract urothelial carcinomas are expected to be cured by surgery.

claim: DNA containing a minimum of 1% neoplastic cells is required for reliable aneuploidy detection.
source: Simulations demonstrated that DNA containing a minimum of 1% neoplastic cells is required for reliable aneuploidy detection, while mutations present in as few as 0.03% of the DNA templates can be detected by the mutation assays used in our study (Bettegowda et al., 2014; Kinde et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's own simulations and is consistent with published literature on aneuploidy detection methods.

claim: Mutations present in as few as 0.03% of DNA templates can be detected by the mutation assays used in the study.

claim: The cost of managing bladder cancer patients under surveillance is in aggregate higher than the cost of managing any other type of cancer, amounting to 3 billion dollars annually.
source: Because urine cytology is relatively insensitive for the detection of recurrence, cystoscopies are performed as often as every three months in such patients in the U.S. In fact, the cost of managing these patients is in aggregate higher than the cost of managing any other type of cancer, amounting to 3 billion dollars annually (Netto and Epstein, 2010).

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutation analysis of UTUC tumors in the study.

source: However, the overall frequency of FGFR3 mutations in our UTUC cohort (21%) was relatively low compared to values reported by Moss et al. (2017) (74%) and Sfakianos et al. (2015) (54%), but was comparable to values reported by Hoang et al., 2013 (8%) and Lee et al. (2018) (13%).

claim: FGFR3 mutation levels are relatively low in upper tract urothelial carcinomas from Han Chinese patients (3-9%) compared to Western patients (36-60%).

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yuan et al. (2016), which provides published evidence for ethnic differences in FGFR3 mutation frequencies.

claim: UroSEEK incorporates massive parallel sequencing assays for mutations in 11 genes and copy number changes on 39 chromosome arms.
source: UroSEEK incorporates massive parallel sequencing assays for mutations in 11 genes and copy number changes on 39 chromosome arms.
evidence: This claim describes the technical design of the UroSEEK assay as implemented in the study.

claim: UroSEEK has three components: detection of intragenic mutations in regions of ten genes, detection of mutations in the TERT promoter, and detection of aneuploidy.
source: UroSEEK has three components: detection of intragenic mutations in regions of ten genes (FGFR3, TP53, CDKN2A, ERBB2, HRAS, KRAS, PIK3CA, MET, VHL and MLL) frequently mutated in urothelial tumors (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Hoang et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2010; Mo et al., 2007; Moss et al., 2017; Netto, 2011; Sarkis et al., 1995; Sarkis et al., 1994; Sarkis et al., 1993; Sfakianos et al., 2015; Wu, 2005); detection of mutations in the TERT promoter (Huang et al., 2013; Killela et al., 2013; Scott et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2016); and detection of aneuploidy (Kinde et al., 2012; Kinde et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim describes the technical design of the UroSEEK assay as implemented in the study, with supporting citations for each component.
